description:
MoviBot recommends up to 3 movies from a curated 238-film Disney/Pixar catalog (feature films, 1940-2017) for requests that mix hard constraints with soft ones. It is a tool-calling agent: an LLM planner is given four tools, ordered cheapest-and-most-exhaustive first, and decides which the question actually needs. CatalogFilter answers from structured columns (year, genre, studio, spoken language, explicit title exclusions). LexicalScreen answers conditions phrased as an absence -- "nobody dies", "nothing scary" -- by scanning every plot passage of every candidate for a word list, which is exhaustive in a way ranking cannot be; searching for "nobody dies" would instead return the films where somebody does. PlotSearch answers from meaning, ranking films by semantic similarity over full plot synopses. SynopsisReader returns the full plot text so the planner can judge claims that no column encodes, such as who betrays whom.

What it CAN do: combine structured and thematic constraints in one query; honour exclusions ("besides Frozen and Moana") as real filters rather than as omissions from the prose; verify story-level properties by reading the plot rather than guessing from genre; and explain why it rejected the obvious alternative.

What it CANNOT do: reason about films outside its catalog (it is a curated Disney/Pixar subset, not all of IMDb); answer anything about films released after 2017, because the underlying dataset is a 2017 snapshot -- it has no knowledge of recent, current, or trending releases and is instructed to refuse such questions rather than answer them from a stale catalog; recommend a short, since everything under 45 minutes was excluded; answer 'movies starring X' or 'directed by Y', as it holds no cast or crew data; and it does not stream or play content. 159 of 238 films are semantically searchable, so a story-level claim about one of the other 79 cannot be verified and it will say so. Where a request is answerable but narrower than the user assumes -- 'recommend a nice comedy' -- it names the universe it is drawing from before recommending, rather than passing a Disney-only pick off as a survey of all cinema.

On completeness: with only 238 films the agent could in principle check every one, but verifying story-level claims means reading full plot texts, so an exhaustive pass would cost far more than any recommendation is worth. Two of its four layers are genuinely exhaustive, though: CatalogFilter and LexicalScreen both check every candidate, so their findings are complete rather than sampled. The other two are not -- PlotSearch returns a top handful and SynopsisReader reads at most 8 plots per call -- which is exactly why the free exhaustive layers run first, shrinking the set before the expensive approximate ones see it. It is instructed to say which kind of finding an answer rests on: a shortlist is the best among the films it looked at, not the best in the catalog. When a request explicitly asks for everything, it lists every film that survived its filters and states what the list is complete with respect to.

Two ranking guardrails are enforced in the data and tool code rather than in the prompt, so no plan can bypass them: shorts under 45 minutes are removed at data-preparation time (they carry very high ratings on very few votes and otherwise dominate every result), and ranking uses a vote-count-weighted Bayesian rating instead of the raw average.
purpose: Answer the kind of movie request that a filter alone cannot: one that combines facts the catalog stores with judgements only the story can settle, and return a single defensible recommendation with the reasoning shown.

prompt_template.template: Query: <a movie request in natural language. It may mix structured constraints (era, genre, studio, language, titles to exclude) with story-level ones (theme, tone, what must or must not happen in the plot, who it is for).>
prompt_template.example: Query: Best empowering princess movie besides Frozen and Moana.

architecture.notes: Module names here match the boxes in /api/model_architecture and the `module` field of every entry in the /api/execute steps trace. Three of the four tools are entirely free and the fourth costs one embedding call (~$0.0000002), because all of them run against local data; only the planner turns cost anything, which is what the turn bound exists to cap. The candidate set is held in Python between calls and never enters the prompt, so films are addressed by "Title (Year)" rather than by id.
architecture.tool_order: Cheapest and most exhaustive first. CatalogFilter narrows 238 films to N on columns; LexicalScreen splits N into clear/flagged/insufficient_text on a word scan; PlotSearch ranks what remains; SynopsisReader reads at most 8. Each layer hands the next a smaller candidate set, so the token-heavy layer only ever sees what survived the free ones.

condition_types.structured: a fact the catalog stores -> CatalogFilter
condition_types.negative: anything phrased as an absence -> LexicalScreen, never PlotSearch
condition_types.semantic: a story, premise or theme stated positively -> PlotSearch
condition_types.narrative: a claim needing to know what happens -> SynopsisReader

prompt_examples.prompt: Best empowering princess movie besides Frozen and Moana.
prompt_examples.expected_tool_path: Planner -> CatalogFilter(keywords=['princess','royalty'], exclude_titles=['Frozen','Moana'], require_synopsis=true) -> Planner -> Final Answer
prompt_examples.verified_tool_output: CatalogFilter matched 13 films, returned best-first by weighted rating: Mulan (1998, 7.42), Beauty and the Beast (1991, 7.38), Aladdin (1992, 7.31), Tangled (2010, 7.30), The Little Mermaid (1989, 7.06). Frozen and Moana are absent because the exclusion was applied as a filter, not left to the prose.
prompt_examples.status: Tool path verified locally at zero cost. The final natural-language response will be captured from the first real planner run once the LLM endpoint is enabled.

prompt_examples.prompt: Something safe for a toddler where nobody dies.
prompt_examples.expected_tool_path: Planner (writes the condition ledger in the same message) -> CatalogFilter(genres=['Animation']) -> LexicalScreen(vocabulary='death') -> Planner -> Final Answer
prompt_examples.verified_tool_output: CatalogFilter matched 90 animated films. LexicalScreen then scanned every plot passage of all 90 for a 37-word death vocabulary and split them: 27 clear, 61 flagged, 2 with too little plot text to screen. The best-rated clear films are Inside Out (7.83), WALL-E (7.73), Toy Story 3 (7.52). The Lion King and Up are flagged, which is correct -- Mufasa and Ellie die, and neither fact appears in any genre, keyword or overview field. Note that flagged means unresolved rather than rejected: a match is often an attempt or a false belief ("believing Woody murdered Buzz"), which is modality rather than vocabulary, so the matching quote comes back with the flag. Two model turns, no embedding call and no synopsis read.
prompt_examples.status: Tool path and every figure above verified locally at zero cost, and asserted by scripts/check_screen.py. The final natural-language response will be captured from a real planner run.
